title: Empirical Evaluation of a Deterministic-Validator Guard for LLM→NetOps Generate→Verify→Repair Pipelines
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study that measured the operational impact of inserting a deterministic network configuration validator into an LLM-driven generate→verify→repair loop for intent→configuration NetOps tasks. Using a reproducible synthetic 200-task multi-vendor intent bank and a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini) under a locked adapter contract (at most one automated repair call per task), each task produced a shared initial candidate and a guarded final artifact after the validator+repair step. The primary estimand was the paired absolute difference in actionable misconfiguration rate (guarded − baseline). Results on N=200 paired tasks: baseline valid-config count 199/200 (success rate 0.995), guarded valid-config count 200/200 (1.000); absolute reduction = 0.005 (0.5 percentage points). Exact McNemar two-sided test p=1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI for the absolute reduction = [0.0, 0.015]. The preregistered primary hypothesis (≥50% reduction) is not supported. Residual actionable errors were extremely rare under this synthetic benchmark and single-model, single-validator setting. We release the full preregistration, execution manifest, per-task scoring traces, and analysis artifacts (hashes in the Disclosure Statement). We discuss operational interpretation, dominant failure-mode observations constrained to the available artifacts, and threats to validity including low baseline error rate, synthetic task scope, single-model evidence, and single-repair limit.

sections.introduction: Motivation. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to automate intent-driven network operations (NetOps) such as translating human intent into vendor-specific device configuration. Prior work has proposed generate→validate→repair architectures and deterministic network validators as operational guardrails, but quantitative evidence about the practical reduction in actionable misconfiguration under a controlled experimental protocol remains limited. Research question. After an autonomy-locked preregistration, we asked: How much does integrating a deterministic network validator into an LLM-driven generate→verify→repair pipeline reduce actionable misconfiguration rates (paired comparison) on a 200-task synthetic multi-vendor NetOps task bank, and what residual error types remain after automated repairs? Contributions. (1) A preregistered paired confirmatory experiment (study id cnsmspec2026_gvr_v1_prereg_001) executed end-to-end with reproducible synthetic tasks and a deterministic validator; (2) public release of execution artifacts and hashes; (3) the empirical result that, for the selected model, validator, and task bank, the absolute reduction in actionable misconfiguration rate was 0.005 (95% CI 0.0–0.015), a null outcome for the preregistered large-effect hypothesis; (4) a focused discussion of operational implications and threats to validity.
sections.related_work: LLM-driven NetOps and intent translation. Recent studies explore LLMs for network configuration generation and intent-based automation (e.g., NetConfEval / NetOps evaluation prototypes) and recommend verification layers to limit risk. Deterministic network analysis. Header Space Analysis and incremental real-time checkers (e.g., NetPlumber) provide formal, deterministic ways to check forwarding and policy properties; such validators are natural guardrails in generate→verify→repair pipelines. Benchmarks and AIOps evaluation. Prior benchmark and survey efforts emphasize the need to measure operational failure modes and the interaction between probabilistic generators and deterministic validators. We cite representative works used for positioning and method design: Kazemian et al. (Header Space Analysis), Khurshid et al. (VeriFlow/NetPlumber), and Wang et al. (NetConfEval). All cited items are verified in the evidence bundle (see Disclosure).
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design. We froze the study plan (cnsmspec2026_gvr_v1_prereg_001) prior to execution. Design: paired binary comparison on N=200 independently generated synthetic intent→configuration tasks stratified across three vendor families (task bank generation and seeds archived). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (final_actionable_error_rate_after_repair − initial_actionable_error_rate). Primary hypothesis (H1): guarded pipeline reduces final actionable misconfiguration rate by ≥50% relative to initial LLM-only outputs (confirmatory). Secondary hypothesis (H2): residual errors after repair are more likely semantic/policy than syntactic (pre-registered). Execution contract. Adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1; model: gpt-5-mini; maximum model calls budgeted 400; actual model_calls_used = 201 (shared initial generation for 200 tasks plus one repair invocation performed by the adapter where permitted). Each task: a shared initial candidate produced by the LLM (baseline), then the deterministic validator examined the candidate; if violations were detected and the adapter permitted, a single automated repair call was allowed (guarded condition). Scoring and validator. A deterministic netops validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) applied full intent-constraint validation and simulator-based semantic checks per task. The validator produced machine-readable per-task traces, final_state snapshots, and categorical score (valid/invalid). Missingness and failures. The preregistered missingness plan specified retries and conservative sensitivity analyses; no model-call failures occurred; complete pairs = 200.
sections.results: Primary confirmatory outcome. After applying the paired analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1) to the archived scoring JSONs: complete_pair_count = 200; baseline valid-configs (no actionable error) = 199; guarded valid-configs = 200. Baseline success rate = 0.995; guarded success rate = 1.000; absolute paired reduction = 0.005 (0.5 percentage points). Paired exact McNemar two-sided test p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI for the absolute reduction = [0.0, 0.015] (bootstrap resamples = 10,000, seed = 1729). Interpretation: the preregistered large-effect threshold (≥50% relative reduction) was not observed; the observed effect is numerically small and statistically non-significant given the discordant-pair structure. Secondary and exploratory outcomes. The study produced per-task validator traces and contamination flags; in this run residual guarded actionable errors = 0, so the secondary confirmatory test (H2) comparing residual error-type proportions could not be meaningfully evaluated from guarded residuals. Execution footprint. Total model calls used = 201; adapter-enforced repair calls per task ≤1; full raw artifacts, per-task scoring JSONs, and salted hashes are available in the execution manifest (paths/hashes given in the Disclosure).
sections.discussion: Practical reading. Under the constrained experimental conditions (synthetic 200-task bank, single hosted model gpt-5-mini, one deterministic validator implementation, single automated repair attempt per task), the deterministic-validator guard produced a numerically tiny absolute reduction because the baseline LLM-generated actionable-error rate was already very low (1/200). This outcome illustrates two operational points: (1) when an LLM is already producing highly accurate configurations for a given synthetic benchmark, the marginal benefit of an automated validator+repair in reducing actionable errors can be small in absolute terms; (2) low observed baseline error rates reduce statistical power to detect moderate-to-large relative improvements. Failure-mode observations (artifact-grounded). The single baseline actionable failure (baseline-only discordant pair count n_01 = 1) was recorded in the per-task scoring JSON and remains available for forensic inspection; after the adapter contract (one repair) the guarded condition produced no actionable failures. We do not generalize beyond these artifacts. Guidance for operators. Deterministic validators remain valuable for auditing, canonicalization, and catching systematic classes of errors that a probabilistic generator might miss; however, the operational ROI depends on baseline LLM error prevalence, validator coverage, repair policy, and the cost model for human verification. Reproducibility. All preregistration and execution artifacts, per-task traces, and analysis outputs are archived with cryptographic hashes (see Disclosure).
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, autonomous confirmatory study measuring the impact of a deterministic validator in an LLM generate→verify→repair NetOps pipeline. On the chosen synthetic 200-task bank with gpt-5-mini and a single deterministic validator/repair adapter, the absolute actionable-misconfiguration reduction was 0.5 percentage points (from 0.5% to 0.0% failure rate), a numerically small effect that does not support the preregistered large-effect hypothesis. The artifacts demonstrate how rigorous preregistration, deterministic validators, and machine-readable scoring can produce reproducible operational evidence; they also show that practical benefit depends strongly on baseline error prevalence, validator scope, model selection, and repair policy. Future work should broaden model diversity, validator implementations, repair budgets, and task realism to map operationally meaningful regimes where validator-assisted repair materially lowers actionable risk. We provide the full execution manifest and hashes to support independent auditing and further experiments (paths and hashes in Disclosure).

limitations: Single-model evidence: only one hosted model variant (gpt-5-mini) was used; results do not imply multi-model generality.

Synthetic task bank and simulator scope: the 200-task benchmark is synthetic and constrained by the generator and deterministic validator semantics; external validity to production networks is limited.
Low baseline error prevalence: baseline actionable-error rate was 1/200, limiting power to detect relative improvements and making effect-size estimates imprecise for rarer failure regimes.
Single automated repair attempt: the adapter contract permitted at most one automated repair per task; the effect of multi-attempt repair loops is unexplored here.
Single deterministic validator implementation: validator coverage gaps or conservative/lenient semantic checks influence measured outcomes; different validators may produce different paired results.
No human-in-the-loop operator placement: the experiment measured fully automated repair under the adapter contract and did not evaluate human approval workflows or HCI costs.
Exploratory analyses: residual failure-mode inferences are constrained by the paucity of guarded failures in this run and are therefore exploratory rather than confirmatory.
